frame: A space station log has drifted down to Twotide Atoll. The Whoshell is puzzled.
text: Captain Abena Osei had been alone on Station Kestrel for two hundred and eleven days, and she had grown used to its sounds: the hum of the air filters, the tick of the cooling pipes, the groan of metal as the station swung into sunlight. The knocking was new. It began on Tuesday, three soft taps behind the wall of the galley, then a pause, then three more. At first she blamed the pipes. By Thursday she had stopped blaming anything and started recording. 'Station log, day 212,' she said into the microphone, keeping her voice steady. 'I can hear knocking inside the walls again. I am not frightened. I would simply like it to stop.' She unscrewed the vent cover with trembling fingers and shone her torch into the dark. Two tiny eyes blinked back at her. A box of seed samples in the cargo hold had been chewed open, and the culprit was a fat brown mouse with sunflower husks stuck to its whiskers. It had stowed away from Earth, eaten its way through four kilograms of seeds and, judging by its size, had been having a wonderful time. Captain Osei laughed so loudly that the mouse dropped its seed. That evening she added a second entry to the log: 'Crew now two. New crew member is small, rude and excellent company.'

text: Vic has played me every Saturday morning outside the Twotide bakery since 1971. I have a dent from the time he dropped me off the ferry, and a second dent from the time he sat on me at a wedding. My valves stick in cold weather, and I sound, as Vic likes to say, 'like a walrus with a head cold'. Last Saturday, though, Vic's hands were too sore to play. He sat on the bench with his thermos while his granddaughter, Mei, lifted me out of the case. She had never played a tuba before. She was nine years old and not much taller than I am. 'I'll just try one note,' she said. She took an enormous breath, pressed her lips to my mouthpiece and blew so hard that a pigeon took off from the bakery roof in fright. It was not a good note. It was, however, extremely loud, and the crowd that had been ignoring us for fifty years suddenly turned to look. Mei blew again, and then again, until the notes began to wobble into something like a tune. By lunchtime, Vic's hat was full of coins. Mei has decided she will play me every Saturday from now on, and I have decided to let her.
